summary: Presents three YANG 1.1 modules for configuring TCP clients and servers, covering basic connection parameters and the client settings needed to go through proxies. They are meant to be reused by models for higher-level protocols such as SSH and TLS, as in RFC 9644 and RFC 9645.

eli5.summary: TCP is how computers hold a steady phone call with each other. This gives a standard set of building blocks for writing down the settings of that call, so other settings lists can reuse them.

subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for configuring TCP clients and servers, including keepalives and SOCKS proxies.

tldr.problem: Protocols that run over TCP, such as SSH and TLS, each need the same basic TCP settings in their management models: addresses, ports, keepalives and, for clients, proxies.
tldr.mechanism: Three YANG 1.1 modules, ietf-tcp-common, ietf-tcp-client and ietf-tcp-server, define groupings that other models reuse with a narrow set of parameters.
tldr.outcome: Higher-level models can drop in a TCP client or server grouping instead of redefining it. The groupings are not deployed on their own, so their security depends on the modules that use them.

today: RFC 9643 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its groupings are used by the SSH and TLS models in RFC 9644 and RFC 9645.

sections.title: Scope of the Three Modules
sections.content:
RFC 9643 defines three YANG 1.1 modules to configure TCP clients and servers (TCP itself is in RFC 9293). They may be used directly or together with the configuration of higher-level protocols such as SSH and TLS, as in RFC 9644 and RFC 9645.

They cover three kinds of base parameters: addresses and port numbers, a reusable grouping for application-specific connection settings such as keepalives, and client settings for traversing proxies. Each module has a very narrow scope and a minimum set of required parameters. Other proxy techniques could be added by augmenting the modules.
sections.eli5: These are three small kits for writing down how a program makes or accepts a TCP connection: where to connect, how to keep the line alive, and whether to go through a go-between.

sections.title: Place in a Family of RFCs
sections.content:
The modules are part of a collection of RFCs that work together to support configuring clients and servers of NETCONF (RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040). In the RFC's dependency diagram, the TCP groupings are used by the SSH, TLS, NETCONF and RESTCONF client-server models, while crypto-types (RFC 9640) is the base of the cryptographic modules.

The RFC states that it complies with the Network Management Datastore Architecture and defines no protocol-accessible nodes that are config false.
sections.eli5: This kit is a base that the SSH and TLS kits snap onto when they need a TCP connection.

sections.title: Common Settings and TCP Keepalives
sections.content:
The ietf-tcp-common module defines tcp-common-grouping, used by both client and server modules. It models TCP keepalives in a keepalives presence container (feature keepalives-supported) with three leaves: idle-time (default 7200 seconds), max-probes (default 9) and probe-interval (default 75 seconds). The container is a presence container because RFC 9293 requires keepalives to be off by default.

The RFC adds guidance. Keepalives SHOULD only be invoked in server applications that might otherwise hang if a client crashes. Idle intervals SHOULD NOT be smaller than 15 seconds, and the probe interval MUST NOT be smaller than one second, with significantly longer values preferred to avoid congestion. A keepalive mechanism MUST NOT treat the failure of any single probe as a dead connection.
sections.eli5: A keepalive is like asking 'are you still there?' on a quiet phone line. Ask too often and you waste effort and clog the line, so the settings let you ask gently and give up only after several tries.

sections.title: The TCP Client Grouping
sections.content:
The ietf-tcp-client module defines tcp-client-grouping. The mandatory remote-address can be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a hostname, and remote-port has neither a default nor a mandatory statement. Modules using the grouping SHOULD refine it, adding a default when the port is well known or marking it mandatory when it must always be configured.

With the local-binding-supported feature, local-address and local-port choose the local end. The default local port is 0, meaning the operating system may pick any available port. A hostname is resolved on each connection attempt, and multiple resulting addresses are tried in local preference order until one connects or all fail.

Keepalives are included through tcp-common-grouping and are gated by the tcp-client-keepalives feature.
sections.eli5: The client settings say who to call, and optionally which of your own phone lines and extension to call from. If you do not pick an extension, the computer chooses one for you.

sections.title: Reaching Servers Through a Proxy
sections.content:
If the proxy-connect feature is supported, an optional proxy-server container lets the client go through a SOCKS proxy. A choice offers Socks4 (the proxy given as an IP address), Socks4a (which also allows a hostname) and Socks5. Each is enabled by its own feature, and the proxy's remote-port defaults to 1080.

For Socks5, an optional authentication-parameters container selects either GSS-API (an empty container for future augmentation) or username and password, which uses the password-grouping from RFC 9640. The Socks5 protocol is in RFC 1928 and its username and password method in RFC 1929.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you cannot call someone directly and must go through a switchboard operator. These settings say which operator to use and what password to give them.

sections.title: The TCP Server Grouping
sections.content:
The ietf-tcp-server module defines tcp-server-grouping. Its core is a local-bind list, keyed by local-address and requiring at least one entry, of the points where the server listens. A server may have several, for example the same port in different address families or different ports in one family.

To listen on all IPv4 addresses the value must be 0.0.0.0 (INADDR_ANY), and for all IPv6 addresses it must be :: (INADDR6_ANY). As with the client, local-port has no default or mandatory statement, so using modules SHOULD refine it. Keepalives are available through the tcp-server-keepalives feature.
sections.eli5: The server settings list the doors where the server waits for visitors. It can have several doors, each with a street address and a door number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules define only groupings and will not be deployed standalone, so their security implications depend on how other modules use them, and designers of importing modules must do their own analysis. They are meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transports and mutual authentication, with access restrictable through NACM (RFC 8341).

One readable node is sensitive: the Socks5 password under username-password. Configuring cleartext passwords is NOT RECOMMENDED, but if one is configured it should never be returned to a client, so the NACM default-deny-all extension is applied to it. No writable node is marked default-deny-write.

Implementations are RECOMMENDED to implement local-binding-supported for cryptographically secure protocols, to allow more granular firewall rules, and it is NOT RECOMMENDED for unsecure protocols, per RFC 6056.
sections.eli5: The only really secret setting here is the password for the go-between. The device is told never to show it back to anyone who asks.

items.title: idle-time
items.text: Default 7200 seconds before the first probe.

items.title: max-probes
items.text: Default 9 failed probes before the peer is assumed gone.

viz.caption: PROXY TYPES THE CLIENT GROUPING OFFERS

items.label: Socks4
items.desc: Proxy is given as an IP address.

items.label: Socks4a
items.desc: Proxy may be given as an IP address or hostname.

items.label: Socks5
items.desc: Hostname allowed, with optional GSS-API or username and password authentication.
